1.  The present claim petition arises out of road accident that occurred on 10.08.2016, in which the petitioner K. Suresh allegedly suffered injuries. An award was passed on 09.07.2020 which was challenged before Hon'ble Delhi High Court. Vide its order dated 08.12.2023, Hon'ble Delhi High Court set aside the award dated 09.07.2020, with directions to assess contributory negligence of the parties to the accident, determine the compensation, if any, payable to the claimant and to determine as to who shall be liable to pay the same.

1 2. The brief facts of the case are that on 10.08.2016, the injured was going towards Lodhi Road on his motorcycle bearing no. DL-7SBZ-2435. When the petitioner was taking a left turn from red light India Habitat Center, Respondent no.2 suddenly opened left side of the door of vehicle number DL-2CAU-7214 (hereinafter referred to as the offending vehicle) in a negligent manner due to which the petitioner was hit and grievously injured on his right foot. At that time, the offending vehicle was being driven by Respondent no.1. 
MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 2 of 22 ss Due to the injury,
petitioner was taken to Safdarjung Hospital for treatment where Respondent no.1 requested him not to lodge any FIR while undertaking to bear all his medical expenses. Petitioner later referred to Kukreja Hospital for further treatment where he underwent surgeries (skin grafting) of his right foot, however Respondent no.1 refused to bear his medical expenses. It is then that the injured /petitioner got registered an FIR no. 154/2016 on 11.08.2016 u/s 337 of IPC at PS Lodhi Colony against the Respondent no.2. 
No DAR has been filed in the case (since the FIR was not registered u/ 279 of IPC), however, the IO upon completion of the investigation filed chargesheet before concerned Ld. MM u/s 337/338 of IPC. 
As per record, Respondent no.1 was the driver of the offending vehicle, Respondent no.2 was his co-passenger, Respondent no.3 is the owner of the offending vehicle and Respondent no. 4 is the insurer of such vehicle.
3. In response to the claim petition, a joint reply was filed by Respondent no.1 and 3 denying the accident to have taken place due to negligence of the offending vehicle. It is pleaded that the offending vehicle was duly insured with Respondent no.4 while Respondent no.1 had a valid driving licence and RC of such vehicle was also valid. It is also pleaded that the alleged accident, infact took place due to negligence of the petitioner. 
No reply of Respondent no.2 and 4 has been found on record (the only written submissions filed by the respondent no.2 and 4 pertain to 13.08.2019 i.e. during final arguments before Ld. MACT No.
37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 3 of 22 ss Predecessor). 
4. After completion of pleadings, following issues were framed on 08.01.2018. 
1. Whether the injured K. Suresh suffered injures in a road traffic accident on 10.08.2016 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. DL-2CAU- 7214 being driven by Respondent no.1, owned by respondent no. 2 and Insured with Respondent no. 3 ? OPP 2. Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP 3. Relief. 
K. Suresh vs Agnibh Mudi on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9853696/ 
2 5. PW-1 petitioner/injured K. Suresh, led his evidence by way of affidavit Ex.PW1/A, reiterating the factum and manner of accident on lines of his claim petition and relied upon RC of the offending vehicle as Ex.PW1/1, driving licence of Respondent no. 1 as Ex.PW1/2, insurance policy as Ex.PW1/3, driving licence of the petitioner as Ex.PW1/4, photographs of injury suffered by petitioner as Ex.PW1/5 (colly), medical bills as Ex.PW1/6 (colly), FIR no. 154/2016 as Ex.PW1/7,
certified copy of the chargesheet as Ex.PW1/8, medical treatment record/bills as Ex.PW1/9, salary certificate as Ex.PW1/10 and his claim petition as Ex.PW1/11. PW-1 was duly cross examined by Ld.
Counsel for Insurance company (Respondent no.4) and the cross examination was adopted by Ld.
Counsel for driver and owner of the offending vehicle (Respondent no. 1 and 3). Respondent no. 2 did not cross examine PW-1. 
MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 4 of 22 ss 6. Respondent no.1 led his evidence by examining himself as R1W1. He tendered his evidence by way of Ex.R1W1/1 and relied upon Insurance policy already Ex.PW1/3, Registration Certificate (RC) of his vehicle already Ex.PW1/1 and his driving licence already Ex.PW1/2.
7. Final arguments in details have been heard afresh, in terms of directions dated 08.12.2023 of Hon'ble Delhi High Court. On the basis of pleadings of the parties, evidence adduced, arguments addressed and directions dated 08.12.2023, issue wise findings are as under:
Whether the injured K. Suresh suffered injures in a road traffic accident on 10.08.2016 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. DL-2CAU-7214 being driven by Respondent no.1, owned by respondent no. 2 and Insured with Respondent no. 3 ? OPP 8. In this issue, the court shall also assess the issue of contributory negligence of the parties to the accident as directed vide order dated 08.12.2023. 
Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law,
proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable. Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & ors. (2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana, MACT No.
37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 5 of 22 ss 2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken. 
9. In the present case, the injured /petitioner has specifically deposed about accident by stating that the accident occurred due to sudden and negligent opening of the left door of the offending vehicle by Respondent no.2. He has deposed that due to the impact, the edge of the frontal door of the offending vehicle pierced the vein of the right foot of the petitioner. During cross- examination of PW-1 it was admitted that the offending vehicle was in a stationery position at the time of the accident and that the petitioner was trying to cross (overtake) the same from its left side. PW-1 K. Suresh vs Agnibh Mudi on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9853696/
3 however, denied that he had hit the offending vehicle on its rear side. A suggestion as to own negligence of petitioner was denied by him. 
Whether the driver of the offending vehicle, Respondent no.1 or Respondent no.2 i.e. co-passenger in the offending vehicle were rash or negligent has to be decided on the basis of the facts and circumstances. The site plan of the incident shows the accident to have occurred a few meters from the red light located in the center of a crossing (leading to 4 different roads) while the road on which the accident took place apparently had a free left cut. Thus, based on the site plan, petitioner cannot be said to have been negligent in plying his motorcycle on the left side of such road, for taking a left turn. At the same time even if the offending vehicle was at halt due to the red light, it is impermissible for any such halting vehicle to deboard any MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 6 of 22 ss passenger sitting therein without indicator or turning the parking lights on. A vehicle halted due to red light cannot be equated with a vehicle parked on the side of the road and as such, the level of precaution expected from the vehicle at halt due to the red light is much more than a vehicle parked on the extreme side of the road. 
The site plan clearly shows that the offending vehicle was not parked on the extreme side of the road nor was there any indicator or parking lights of such vehicle switched on. No person plying on the road could have reasonably expected that the door of such halted vehicle would suddenly open. The driver of the offending vehicle was certainly at fault in halting the vehicle in defiance of the traffic signal and for deboarding its passenger. In fact the offending vehicle is VXI model of Swift Car which is enabled with an automatic locking system of the doors of the car once the car starts plying on the road at a minimum speed. After the doors of the car are automatically locked, the same can only be opened either by the driver of the car from the centralized locking system of the car or manually, by the passenger. Respondent no. 1 has nowhere taken a defence or pleaded that Respondent no.2 had opened the lock of the door without his knowledge and as such it is presumed that Respondent no.2 was deboarding the offending vehicle with consent or atleast knowledge of Respondent no.1. Undoubtedly, the accident has occurred due to sudden opening of the door of an unauthorizedly parked or halted vehicle. In these circumstances, Respondent no.1 failed in his duties by allowing Respondent no.2 to deboard the car in the middle of the road, MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 7 of 22 ss while the car was at halt on the traffic signal,
without cautioning her as to the risk involved. 
10. By entering into the witness box, Respondent no.1 has testified as R1W1 that he had rightfully stopped his car at a temporary auto stand and a semi circular area de-marketed for auto stand or halting of any moving vehicle. He has simultaneously asserted that he had halted his car 100 meters away from the red light to enable his friend /Respondent no.2 to alight. There is however no indication in the site plan nor any proof of any auto stand being at the spot of accident, filed by Respondent no.1. Contrary stand taken by R1W1 with regard to halting of his vehicle either at the red light or at an alleged 'temporary' auto stand renders his defence unreliable. 
11. It is a settled law that the word 'use' under the Motor Vehicle Act, has a wider connotation and covers a situation even where the motor vehicle is not moving and is stationary (Ref. Shivaji Dayanu Patil & anr. v. Vatschala Uttam More, 1991 3SCC 530). 
K. Suresh vs Agnibh Mudi on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9853696/
4 12. In the present case, police after investigation had filed chargesheet against Respondent no. 2 u/s 337/338 of IPC which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent No. 2 in causing the accident. 
However, mere non registration of a criminal case against Respondent no.1, would not exonerate him of his liability under the Motor Vehicle Act. Further, under the Motor Vehicle Act, Respondent no.3 i.e. the owner of the offending vehicle is MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. 
Page no. 8 of 22 ss also vicariously liable while the insurer is liable by virtue of the insurance policy i.e. contractual liability to indemnify Respondent no. 3.
13. Accordingly, Issue no. 1 is decided in favour of the petitioner. 
Issue no. 2 Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP.
14. Respondent no.4 has taken no statutory defence in the case. As per record the driving licence of Respondent no.1 was valid on the date of accident and the registration certificate as well as insurance policy was effective on the date of accident. From the discussion held in issue no.1 and from the facts and circumstances of the case, a contributory negligence of 70% is attributable on Respondent no.1 while 30% negligence was on the part of Respondent no.2. For negligence of Respondent no.1 and 2, Respondent no.3 is vicariously liable being owner of the vehicle, however by virtue of contract of Insurance, Respondent no.4 is liable to indemnify the respondents. As such,
Respondent no. 4 is liable to pay compensation to the petitioner. 
15. Now as regards the issue of quantum of compensation, this court relies upon the judgments of C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair, R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) MACT No.
37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 9 of 22 ss Ltd. and Baker v. Willoughby which are referred and relied in Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 Supreme Court cases 343 decided by Hon'ble SC wherein it has been observed that the provision of the Motor Vehicles Act,
1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident. The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. 
16. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)

5 (i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure;
MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 10 of 22 ss (ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising;
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability;
(iii) Future medical expenses. 
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
16.1. In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a)
and (iv). 16.2. It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
(v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life. 
16.3. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under Item (ii) (a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence. 
16.4. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs.
Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 11 of 22 ss further treatment and cost thereof. 
16.5. Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of l u m p s u m a m o u n t s w i t h r e f e r e n c e t o c i r c u m s t a n c e s s u c h a s a g e , n a t u r e o f injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. Decisions of Hon'ble SC and Hon'ble High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary. 
K. Suresh vs Agnibh Mudi on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9853696/
6 16.6. It was observed by Apex Court in such case of Raj Kumar (supra) that what usually poses some difficulty is the assessment of the loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability--Item (ii) (a).
16.7. We are not concerned with assessment regarding loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability in this case, as petitioner did not suffer any permanent disability. 
17. The MLC of the victim prepared at Safdarjung Hospital reveals that the petitioner suffered a lacerated wound over dorsal aspect of right leg of size 5X3 cm with tender injury. There is no opinion as to injury being grievous in nature. There is no referral of the patient by the concerned doctor to a higher center. It appears that the petitioner voluntarily got himself admitted in another hospital on 10.08.2016 and remained admitted for two days. There is no denial of the fact that the petitioner has obtained treatment from Kukreja Hospital, which is evident from the medical treatment papers as well as bills. 
18. Now in order to assess the loss of income suffered by the MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs.
Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 12 of 22 ss petitioner, his monthly income/salary has to be assessed. 
Petitioner has claimed to be working as a clerk with one Nakul Mohta, advocate Supreme Court of India from where he drew a salary of Rs.15,000/- per month. Petitioner has relied upon a salary certificate issued by his employer which is Ex.PW1/10. The quantum of his salary has been disputed by Ld. Counsel for the Insurance company. During cross-examination of PW-1, he has admitted that he used to receive his salary through Bank transfer but has failed to file his bank account statement to show its receipts. Despite it being disputed by Ld. Counsel for Respondent no.4 by putting a negative suggestion as to being employed with Mr. Nakul Mohta, advocate, petitioner has not examined his employer to prove his employment or receipt of salary to the tune of Rs.15,000/-. The salary certificate so relied does not specify the post or position at which the petitioner was working,
if he was so working. Petitioner has also not filed any document to prove his educational or professional qualifications, in absence of which, the court is constrained to assume his income on the basis of minimum wages of an unskilled labour prevailing in Delhi (though no address proof of Delhi has been filed by the petitioner, but assuming on the basis of undisputed averment) at the time of accident i.e. as on 10.08.2016 of Rs.9568/-. 
Further, petitioner has not filed any proof to show the number of days he was incapable of attending his work due to the injury. Keeping in view the nature of injury, it is assumed that the petitioner may not have been able to attend his work for at least 15 days and thus, loss of his income is to be calculated MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 13 of 22 ss accordingly.

25. At this stage, it is relevant to the refer to the judgment of A. V. Padma & Ors. Vs., R. Venugopal &

9 Even as per the guidelines issued by this Court Court, long term fixed deposit of amount of compensation is mandatory only in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows. In the case of illiterate claimants, the Tribunal is allowed to consider the request for lumpsum payment for effecting purchase of any movable property such as agricultural implements, rickshaws etc. to earn a living. However, in such cases, the Tribunal shall make sure that the amount is actually spent for the purpose and the demand is not a ruse to withdraw money. In the case of semi-illiterate claimants,
the Tribunal should ordinarily invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. But if the Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 17 of 22 ss Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid. In the case of literate persons, it is not mandatory to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. 
The expression used in guideline No. (iv) issued by this Court is that in the case of literate persons also the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i), whereas in the guideline Nos. (i), (ii), (iii) and (v), the expression used is that the Tribunal should. Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i) only if,
having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. 
Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the compensation amount in long term fixed deposit and to release even the whole amount in the case of literate persons. However, the Tribunals are often taking a very rigid stand and are mechanically ordering in almost all cases that the amount of compensation shall be invested in long term fixed deposit. They are taking such a rigid and mechanical approach without understanding and appreciating the distinction drawn by this Court in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows and in the case of semiliterate and literate persons. It needs to be clarified that the above guidelines were issued by this Court only to safeguard the interests of the claimants, particularly the minors, illiterates and others whose amounts are sought to be withdrawn on some fictitious grounds. The guidelines were not to be understood to mean that the Tribunals were to take a rigid stand while considering an application seeking release of the money. 
The guidelines cast a responsibility on the Tribunals to pass appropriate orders after examining each case on its own merits. However, it is seen that even in cases when there is no possibility or chance of the feed being frittered away by the beneficiary owing to ignorance, illiteracy or susceptibility to exploitation, investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit is directed by the Tribunals as a matter of course and in a routine manner, ignoring the object and the spirit of the guidelines issued by MACT No. 37/2017 K. Suresh vs. Agnibh Mudi & ors. Page no. 18 of 22 ss this Court and the genuine requirements of the claimants. Even in the case of literate persons, the Tribunals are automatically ordering investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed K. Suresh vs Agnibh Mudi on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9853696/
10 deposit without recording that having regard to the age or fiscal background or the strata of the society to which the claimant belongs or such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks it necessary to direct such investment in the larger interests of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded to him.
The Tribunals very often dispose of the claimant's application for withdrawal of the amount of compensation in a mechanical manner and without proper application of mind. This has resulted in serious injustice and hardship to the claimants. The Tribunals appear to think that in view of the guidelines issued by this Court, in every case the amount of compensation should be invested in long term fixed deposit and under no circumstances the Tribunal can release the entire amount of compensation to the claimant even if it is required by him. Hence a change of attitude and approach on the part of the Tribunals is necessary in the interest of justice..."
